components.description: A global, keyboard-first overlay (⌘K/Ctrl+K) for finding resources and running actions across an app. Renders as a centered floating panel on desktop and a full-width sheet under the sm breakpoint. Exports CommandMenu (the controlled root), CommandMenuInput, CommandMenuList (which auto-renders a live result-count announcer), CommandMenuEmpty, CommandMenuGroup, CommandMenuSeparator, and CommandMenuItem (accepts onSelect, an optional leading icon, and an optional keybind hint rendered as a kbd badge). Composes cmdk for the ARIA combobox/filter engine under a Radix Dialog for focus trapping, portalling and dismiss-on-escape/outside-click, with a token-driven CSS fade+scale for entrance/exit. Controlled-only: there is no internal open state, because the global shortcut listener has to live in the host app regardless. Use for apps with enough destinations or repeat actions that menu-hunting has real cost — dashboards, admin panels, developer tools; do not use it for a menu triggered from one visible button or row, use a Menu or ContextMenu instead.

open.description: Controlled open state. There is no uncontrolled fallback — see engineeringNotes.

label.description: Accessible dialog name. Not visible; announced once when the menu opens.

icon.description: Leading icon, muted by default so it recedes behind the label. size-4 recommended.

keybind.description:
Rendered visibly in the row and, because it stays in the item's text flow rather
than an aria-hidden decoration, announced as part of the option's accessible name —
satisfying "hotkeys are both visible and announced" without extra ARIA wiring.

UINode.description: A nested component: a name from this catalogue, and the props to give it.

props.description: That component's own props, matching its entry in this catalogue.

guidance.engineering: Uses cmdk for the input/list/filter engine rather than hand-rolling the ARIA combobox contract (input keeps DOM focus while aria-activedescendant points at the highlighted listbox option) — that contract is easy to get subtly wrong and cmdk is the same engine Vercel's own Geist command menu and shadcn/ui's command component build on. Radix Dialog wraps the whole thing rather than cmdk's own Command.Dialog variant, so PixelDosa keeps ownership of the visual contract instead of inheriting cmdk's default dialog chrome. Deliberately does NOT compose the shared `overlay` primitive (Motion-driven), despite that being the original plan: `overlay`'s AnimatePresence usage has a confirmed upstream bug (motiondivision/motion#3243) where the exiting panel and its full-viewport scrim sometimes never unmount, permanently blocking further page interaction after the first close — reproduced independently in Overlay's own existing demo, in both dev and production builds, so it is a primitive-level defect, not a composition mistake here. This component instead drives its fade+scale with a plain two-phase (mount in the closed state, flip to open on the next animation frame) CSS transition gated by a deterministic `setTimeout`-based delayed-unmount hook, reading the same `--pd-duration-fast`/`--pd-ease-standard` tokens `overlay` uses, so the visual result is identical while sidestepping the bug entirely. Recommend re-composing `overlay` here once its exit-completion issue is fixed upstream or worked around at the primitive level. Controlled-only open state (no internal fallback) because the consumer's global keydown listener already has to own the boolean. Also works around a second, unrelated composition gotcha: cmdk's own keydown handling on the Command root prevents Escape from reaching Radix's document-level dismissable-layer listener when cmdk is composed manually instead of via its own Command.Dialog, so Escape-to-close is handled explicitly rather than left to Radix alone. The result-count aria-live announcer is rendered automatically inside CommandMenuList via cmdk's useCommandState hook rather than left for every consumer to wire up. A separate kbd primitive was considered (per the component plan) and deliberately deferred: the keybind badge is a few lines of markup used only inside CommandMenuItem for v1, and extracting it into its own registry item before a second consumer needs it would be speculative.
guidance.motion: Fade (opacity) plus a slight scale-in (0.98 → 1) on both the scrim and panel, matching the shared overlay primitive's visual signature even though it isn't composed directly here (see engineeringNotes). Mounts in the closed state, then flips to the open data-state on the next animation frame so the browser actually has a 'from' value to transition from — setting both in the same commit would skip the transition entirely. Duration and easing come from --pd-duration-fast/--pd-ease-standard, the same tokens Overlay uses, so the timing stays in step with the rest of the system. Exit is handled by a matching deterministic delay (150ms, comfortably above the fast token) before the panel actually leaves the DOM, so the fade-out is never cut short. The mobile sheet layout (full-width, pinned near the viewport bottom under the sm breakpoint) intentionally keeps the same fade+scale rather than a directional slide-from-bottom, per the component plan's call to reuse one motion signature rather than add a second pattern for one breakpoint. Highlighted-row background change on CommandMenuItem uses --pd-duration-instant with --pd-ease-standard, matching Button's press-feedback timing, because it is state feedback rather than decoration. Under prefers-reduced-motion, both the panel/scrim transition and the row-highlight transition are removed via motion-reduce:transition-none (scale pinned to 100% via motion-reduce:scale-100), leaving the opacity and background-colour changes themselves intact so every state change stays legible without motion.

components.name: compare-view
components.title: Compare View
components.description: Before and after, without the usual accessibility failure. Takes `before` and `after`, each with your own `content` and a required `label` that doubles as its description, a starting `view` of `slider` or `side`, `allowViewChange`, an `aspectRatio` so nothing jumps while media loads, and an optional `onChoose` returning `before` or `after`. The slider is a native `input[type=range]`, which is the point: comparison sliders in AI editing tools are almost all mouse-only, built from pointer maths with no keyboard path and no announcement, while a range input gives arrow keys, Home and End, touch, and a labelled value screen readers can read ("60% AI edit, clear sky"). The after side is clipped rather than resized, so both halves stay pixel-aligned, and side-by-side is one click away for anyone who would rather see both at once. Purely presentational: you render both sides. Use it for edits, upscales, restorations and style transfers. Not for several results of one prompt (that is Variation Grid), and not for text, which needs Diff Accept.

headingLevel.description: Level of the title heading, so it fits the outline of the page it's placed in. Defaults to 3.

before.description: What it was. Give it a real description: this is also its alt text.

after.description: What the AI made of it.

view.description: Start in `slider` (one image, a handle) or `side` (both, at once).

allowViewChange.description: Locks the view when your layout only fits one of them.

aspectRatio.description: Aspect ratio of the frame, so nothing jumps while the media loads.

UINode.description: A nested component: a name from this catalogue, and the props to give it.

props.description: That component's own props, matching its entry in this catalogue.

events.name: onChoose
events.description: Keeps whichever one the person picks.

guidance.engineering: The slider is a real range input for one reason that outweighs the styling cost: every keyboard, touch and assistive-technology behaviour comes from the platform, and the custom handles these tools ship are the single most common accessibility failure in AI editing UIs. Revealing is done with `clip-path` on an absolutely positioned overlay rather than by resizing the after side, because resizing re-lays-out the media and the two halves drift apart by a pixel or two at every step — visible exactly where people are looking for differences. `aria-valuetext` counts down from the slider value — the handle is the divider, so a higher value uncovers *less* of the new image — and names the side it is measuring, so the announcement matches the screen instead of contradicting it. Labels are required rather than optional on both sides, since a comparison whose halves are unlabelled is meaningless to anyone not looking at it.
guidance.motion: Nothing animates. The handle follows the input directly with no easing, because a comparison is a direct-manipulation surface where a lagging reveal reads as broken rather than smooth. The view toggle changes layout instantly for the same reason, and `prefers-reduced-motion` has nothing to disable.

components.name: confidence-meter
components.title: Confidence Meter
components.description: A tiered (low/medium/high) confidence indicator with an optional provenance caption, shared by every AI-tier component that needs to communicate uncertainty about a proposed value, classification, or decision. Renders a three-bar filled/unfilled indicator (1/2/3 bars for low/medium/high) immediately followed by a text label ('Low confidence', 'Medium confidence', 'High confidence') — never a raw percentage, since that would claim precision the underlying model doesn't actually have. An optional provenance string renders as a second 'via {provenance}' caption alongside the tier. Purely presentational: no state, no async behaviour, a pure function of its props. Use anywhere an AI-proposed value or decision carries a confidence signal (Smart Field, Diff Accept, Selection Actions, and the future AI Approval Gate all compose this rather than each re-deriving their own indicator). Not for a full sources/context/explanation surface — use AI Context / Provenance Surface for that instead.

provenance.description: Optional source caption, rendered as "via {provenance}" alongside the tier.

guidance.engineering: Extracted from two already-shipped components (Smart Field, Selection Actions) that had independently hand-rolled the identical tiered indicator — the concrete signal per the system's own 'a component is not an island' rule that this belongs as its own primitive rather than being re-derived a third time. Confidence is a three-tier enum, not a raw number, by deliberate and unchanged decision from Smart Field's original plan: a fabricated percentage would claim precision the model doesn't actually have, and the system's token set has no 'success'/'warning' hue to spend on a red/yellow/green scale anyway — only `destructive` keeps real chroma. A numeric-score-to-tier bucketing input was considered and deferred: no current consumer has a raw calibrated score to map, and adding that path now would solve a hypothetical need rather than an observed one. Provenance is folded into this component as an optional prop rather than left as a sibling element every consumer composes separately, since the two already-shipped call sites both rendered them side by side anyway — one import now covers both.
guidance.motion: None, deliberately. This is a static presentational primitive with no state transitions of its own — any entrance/exit motion belongs to whatever container shows it (e.g. Smart Field's proposal panel), the same way Card's motion belongs to whatever wraps it, not to the primitive itself. Nothing here required a component-specific motion or reduced-motion branch, which is itself a signal the component is doing exactly what it needs to and no more.

components.name: cost-estimate
components.title: Cost Estimate
components.description: What a run will cost and how long it will take, shown before it starts. Takes a `cost` range (`low` and optional `high`, formatted by you in money or credits), an optional `duration` in plain words, a `confidence` tier from Confidence Meter, a `basis` naming where the estimate comes from, an `items` breakdown of what the spend is made of, and a `balance` with the user's remaining budget or credits — including `exceeds` when this run would go past it, which is stated before the button rather than after. A range is the default shape on purpose: a single confident figure claims precision an estimate doesn't have, and the confidence is a tier rather than a percentage for the same reason. Purely presentational and provider-free: you compute the numbers from your own pricing and history and pass them in formatted, so the component never guesses a currency, a model price or a token count. Holds completely still — it is the user's turn. Use it before a costly or long run, beside Intent Preview or Agent Plan. Not for live spend during a run, not for a billing page, and not for showing raw token counts, which are not a unit people can judge.

headingLevel.description: Level of the title heading, so it fits the outline of the page it's placed in. Defaults to 3.

task.description: What the run is, in the user's words: "Research the top 5 competitors".

cost.description: What it will spend. A range is the honest shape of an estimate.

duration.description: How long it will take: "about 3 to 5 minutes". Plain words, not a countdown.

confidence.description:
How good the estimate is. Tiers, never a percentage: an estimate that claims
precision it doesn't have is worse than no estimate.

basis.description: Where the estimate comes from: "your last 20 runs".

items.description: What the spend is made of. Shown as a short list, never a chart.

label.description: "1,250 credits left", "$18.40 of $50 left".

used.description: 0–1, measured. Renders a bar; leave it out when you only have words.

exceeds.description: Set when this run would take them past their budget.

balance.description: What's left, if the user has a budget or a credit balance.

low.description: Formatted by you, in your currency or unit: "$1.20", "600 credits".

high.description: Leave out for a single figure you're sure of.

label.description: "Reads 240 pages", "12 image generations".

amount.description: What it costs, already formatted by you: "$0.40", "120 credits", "~2 min".

guidance.engineering: The API refuses the two lies this surface usually tells. First, a single figure: `cost` is a range, and a caller who genuinely knows the price passes only `low`, which makes precision an explicit choice rather than the default. Second, a percentage of certainty: confidence reuses the shipped three-tier Confidence Meter instead of inventing a number, and `basis` names the evidence so the estimate can be judged. Everything arrives pre-formatted as strings because currency, locale and credit units belong to the host product; a component that formatted money would have to guess a currency and would be wrong in half the places it renders. The only proportion drawn is the budget bar, which comes from a measured `used` value — the same rule the rest of the system applies to progress. `exceeds` is a separate flag rather than something derived from the numbers, because only the caller knows whether the estimate's high end, the low end, or an average is the figure that counts against a budget.
guidance.motion: Nothing moves. This is the user's turn in the fullest sense — a decision about money — so the component holds completely still, with no shimmer, pulse or progress. The only transitions are the standard instant colour changes on its buttons, and those are disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

components.name: credits-meter
components.title: Credits Meter
components.description: What's left, and what this will cost — before the click. Takes the `remaining` balance and optional `allowance`, both formatted by you, a measured `used` proportion, a `nextAction` naming the action and its `cost` together with `affordable` when it exceeds the balance, `resets` for when the balance renews or expires, `recent` for movement including refunds, `low` to mark a balance worth flagging, and `onTopUp`. The pairing of action and price is the point: buyers of these tools rank credit opacity as their first frustration, and the specific complaint is that you cannot tell what an action will cost until it has been spent. Purely presentational: you compute the numbers and format the units. Use it beside a generate button, in a studio's sidebar, or above a batch. Not a billing page, and not a place for raw token counts — convert to the unit your users are charged in.

remaining.description: What's left, formatted by you: "1,250 credits", "$18.40".

allowance.description: The full allowance, when there is one: "2,000 credits this month".

used.description:
How much of the allowance is already spent, 0–1, measured. Renders a bar; leave it
out when you only have words. The bar draws what is *left*, so it empties as the
figure beside it falls.

nextAction.description:
What the next action will take, named and priced: the thing reviewers say is missing
everywhere. "4 images · 40 credits".

resets.description: When the balance resets or expires, in plain words: "Resets on 1 October".

recent.description: Recent movement, including refunds: "12 refunded yesterday when a batch failed".

low.description: Set when the balance is low enough to say so.

guidance.engineering: `nextAction` is a single object rather than separate label and cost props so the two can never be rendered apart: a price with no action, or an action with no price, is the pattern the component exists to replace. `affordable` is a caller flag instead of something derived from parsing the strings, because balances and costs arrive as formatted text in whatever unit and locale the product uses, and a component that tried to compare them would have to parse money. The bar is drawn only from a measured `used` value, which keeps it consistent with the rest of the system's rule that a proportion must be real, and it draws what is *left* rather than what is spent: it sits under a figure that counts down, and a bar filling up beside a balance running out reads as plenty-left at the exact moment it is not. Refunds get a place in `recent` because generation pipelines refund routinely and almost no interface shows it, which leaves people believing failures cost them money.
guidance.motion: Nothing animates. A balance is a fact and the next action's price is a decision point, so neither has anything to express through motion; only the standard instant colour change on the top-up button, disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

components.name: diff-accept
components.title: Diff Accept
components.description: Reviews an AI-proposed text change as an inline word-level diff, resolved hunk by hunk rather than all-or-nothing. Takes baseValue (the text the proposal was generated against), value (the current live value), and proposedValue (the AI's suggested replacement), and computes the diff between baseValue and proposedValue using the diff (jsdiff) library. Each contiguous run of changed words becomes one hunk with its own Accept/Reject controls, shown inline as struck-through removed text and underlined/tinted added text. If value no longer matches baseValue — the underlying text changed since the proposal was generated — the diff is not shown; a conflict banner renders instead with an optional onRegenerate callback. Apply commits the current resolution (accepted hunks use the proposed text, pending or rejected hunks keep the original) via onApply, with a brief Undo affordance after. Use for reviewing AI rewrites of existing text — a bio, a description, any content field — where accepting some proposed changes and rejecting others is a real, expected outcome. Not for a single atomic value with no internal structure to partially accept — use smart-field for that.

baseValue.description: The text the proposal was generated against. Compared to `value` to detect conflicts.

value.description: The current live value. If it no longer matches `baseValue`, a conflict banner renders instead of the diff.

undoWindowMs.description: How long the Undo affordance stays visible after applying, in ms.

events.name: onApply
events.description: Fires with the merged result once the user applies their resolutions.

events.name: onRegenerate
events.description: Shown on conflict instead of the diff. Typically re-requests a fresh proposal against the current value.

guidance.engineering: Uses diff (jsdiff) for the actual word-level diff computation rather than hand-rolling a diff algorithm — the same relationship command-menu has with cmdk: a solved problem with real edge cases (Unicode, whitespace runs, word-boundary detection) not worth re-solving here. Hunks are grouped from the raw diff parts by merging consecutive added/removed runs into one reviewable unit, so a 'replace X with Y' shows as a single hunk with both the removal and the replacement, not two separate uncoordinated changes. Unresolved (pending) hunks default to the original text when merging, never the proposed one — an AI change only lands in the final result if a hunk is explicitly accepted, matching the system-wide 'never silently commit' rule. The status model is a three-state machine (reviewing/applied/done) rather than a single boolean: collapsing 'applied' and 'done' into one flag caused a real bug during development, where the conflict check (value !== baseValue, which becomes true immediately after Apply changes the live value) would incorrectly override the Undo affordance and show a conflict banner instead — the fix was ordering status checks so 'applied'/'done' short-circuit before the conflict check ever runs, since conflict is only a meaningful question while still reviewing.
guidance.motion: The system has no 'success'/'added' hue — destructive is the only token keeping real chroma — so additions and removals are distinguished primarily by text decoration (strikethrough for removed, underline plus a bg-accent/40 tint for added), not a red/green colour scheme, with destructive reserved for the removed text only since deletion is the one case that's legitimately danger-adjacent. This is also more accessible than colour alone, not just a token-budget workaround. Colour and background transitions on hunk resolution use --pd-duration-instant/--pd-ease-standard, matching Button's press-feedback timing, since resolving a hunk is an immediate state confirmation. Apply's brief settle state mirrors Smart Field's accept feedback for the same component family consistency. Under prefers-reduced-motion, all colour and background transitions drop via motion-reduce:transition-none, leaving the underlying decoration (strikethrough/underline) and resolved text fully legible without animation.

components.name: draft-mode
components.title: Draft Mode
components.description: The agent prepares everything and nothing leaves until a person sends it. Takes `enabled` with `onEnabledChange` for the mode itself, the `items` the agent has prepared (each with a `title` phrased as the consequence, an optional `target` naming who or what it touches, a `detail`, and `irreversible` for anything that can't be taken back), then `onSend`, `onDiscard` and `onEdit`. Items are chosen explicitly with checkboxes; the send button names the count, the line beside it says how many of the chosen items can't be undone, and nothing is ever sent by a single glance-and-click. With the mode off, a still, orange-marked strip states what now happens instead and offers to turn it back on. It is the opposite failure mode to an approval dialog: an approval interrupts once per action and trains people to click through, while draft mode lets the agent work and collects the output for one review at a time the person chooses. Holds completely still — everything here is the user's turn. Use it for agents that send email, post, publish or change live data. Not for a single high-risk action awaiting a decision (that is AI Approval Gate), and not for reviewing many AI-proposed edits row by row (that is AI Triage Table).

headingLevel.description: Level of the title heading, so it fits the outline of the page it's placed in. Defaults to 3.

enabled.description: On: the agent prepares everything and nothing leaves until the user sends it.

items.description: What's waiting. Empty is a normal, quiet state.

offWarning.description: What happens with draft mode off, in your product's words.

title.description: What it is, as the consequence of sending it: "Email Dana about the renewal".

target.description: Who or what it touches: "dana@acme.com", "3 recipients", "the live pricing page".

irreversible.description: Marks an item that can't be taken back once it goes.

events.name: onSend
events.description: Sends the chosen items. Phrase your confirmation as the consequence.

guidance.engineering: Selection is the component's only state, and it is pruned against `items` on every change: an id that has left the list is dropped, because a stale id surviving in the selection is exactly how a batch action sends the wrong thing. There is no accept-all shortcut hiding behind a single control — 'Select all' is a visible, reversible selection step before the send, and the send button carries the count so the action names its own size. Irreversibility is counted from the chosen items rather than shown per row only, so the sentence under the button changes as the selection changes and the warning cannot be scrolled past. The mode switch is a real `role="switch"` with an explanatory sentence that rewrites itself for each state, instead of a settings label that leaves people guessing what 'off' does; turning it off does not hide the consequence, it states it in the waiting colour and offers the way back.
guidance.motion: Nothing animates except the switch itself, which slides its thumb over `--pd-duration-fast` so the state change reads as a physical flip rather than a repaint. No item pulses, shimmers or slides in: this surface is entirely the user's turn, and motion here would imply the agent is still doing something. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the switch transition is dropped and the state is carried by position, colour and the word On or Off.

components.name: field
components.title: Field
components.description: A composable form-field wrapper providing Field, FieldLabel, FieldControl, FieldDescription and FieldError parts that share one generated id set and automatically wire aria-describedby and aria-invalid onto whatever control is placed inside FieldControl. Has no opinion on form-state management — works with plain useState, react-hook-form, or any other library. Use it as the base every labeled input, textarea or custom control composes on top of; it is the primitive that GhostInput, SmartField and every other AI-in-product component in this system builds on.

id.description: Base id for the control. A stable id is generated if omitted.

invalid.description: Marks the field as invalid — the control gets aria-invalid and the error styles apply.

guidance.engineering: Built as a compound-component set sharing React context rather than a single Field component with many props, because form fields have a genuinely variable shape (some have descriptions, some don't; some controls are custom comboboxes, not <input>) and a large prop-driven API would force every consumer through the same limited combinations. FieldControl clones its child instead of rendering its own DOM node specifically so that input+icon or input+button compositions keep their existing layout — a wrapper div would break those. FieldDescription and FieldError register their presence into context via an effect so FieldControl's aria-describedby is always accurate even when a description or error mounts after the control, which happens constantly with async validation.
guidance.motion: No motion. This is a compound primitive other components render inside of, not a state that changes visibly on its own — anything Field itself animated would be inherited (and likely duplicated) by every component built on top of it. Error text appearing or disappearing is the one plausible candidate for a transition; it is left as a plain instantaneous swap here so that a consumer building a specific validation UX (e.g. GhostInput's inline error) chooses its own timing rather than inheriting one that might not fit.

components.name: generation-job
components.title: Generation Job
components.description: A generation that takes minutes, told honestly. Takes a `status` (`queued`, `running`, `partial`, `done`, `failed`, `cancelled`), the `title` of what's being made, a `queue` with `position` and the `typicalWait` at this moment, the current `stage` as replaceable text, a **measured** `progress` (leave it out and no bar is drawn), `startedAt` for a self-ticking elapsed counter, the `cost` and your `refundNote` stated before anything fails, an `error` carrying both the reason and what happened to the money, and a `notify` toggle so nobody has to watch the screen. Finished outputs are children and appear the moment they exist, so a batch where two of four are ready shows two. Purely presentational and provider-free: you own the job, the queue and the refunds. Use it for image, video, audio or long document generation. Not for sub-second work (that is Generation Placeholder), and not for an agent run with steps (that is Agent Plan).

Measured progress, 0–1. Leave it out while the extent is unknown: an invented bar is

cost.description: What it costs, formatted by you: "12 credits".

guidance.engineering: Built against the complaints this category actually generates: reviews of image and video tools rank credits and unexplained waits above quality, and queue times of ten to thirty minutes at peak are normal. So the queue is a first-class state with a position and a typical wait rather than a spinner; `progress` is optional and a bar is drawn only when it is passed, because an invented bar on a job whose extent is unknown is the same lie as fake typing; `partial` exists as a status so a batch with two of four finished can show two, which the pipeline literature treats as the correct outcome rather than a pass or fail; and `error` carries a refund string beside the reason, because a failure that silently keeps someone's credits is the complaint underneath most one-star reviews. The elapsed counter ticks inside the component — the one place this system breaks its caller-owns-async rule — so a minutes-long job doesn't force a re-render a second on the consumer.
guidance.motion: Motion means the machine is busy. The status dot pulses while queued, running or partial, the stage verb shimmers while work is ongoing, and every bit of it stops the moment the job reaches a terminal state. A measured bar animates its width over `--pd-duration-slow` with a linear ease, because it tracks real progress rather than decorating a wait. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the pulse and shimmer are dropped and the state is carried by the words and the colour.

components.name: generation-placeholder
components.title: Generation Placeholder
components.description: A layout-reserving placeholder for AI-generated media — image, video, or audio — that encodes real generation progress as a resolving dot field and then cross-fades into the finished artifact. Takes `status` (`queued` | `generating` | `processing` | `done` | `failed`), an optional `progress` between 0 and 1, a required `aspectRatio` that reserves the artifact's final bounds, and a `label` used as both the visible and announced status text. Renders its children only once `status` is `done`, so the component is a container rather than a sibling that gets swapped out — which is what prevents a layout shift at the moment the artifact appears. Two forms share one rendering engine: `field` draws a dot grid for image and video, `bars` draws a row of vertical bars for audio, where a rectangle of dots would misrepresent the medium. Progress is encoded spatially rather than temporally: every cell holds a stable pseudo-random threshold and resolves once progress passes it (ordered-dither logic), so the pattern itself carries the information and stays fully legible with all animation removed. `progress` is optional and never fabricated — omit it and the component shows an honest indeterminate wave rather than a synthetic percentage creeping toward 90%. Use it anywhere media is being generated. Not for streaming text (use Progressive Reveal, which appends whole items rather than refining in place), not for agent activity with no artifact attached, and not as a generic content skeleton — this component exists precisely because media generation progress is measurable, and a skeleton discards that.

progress.description:
0–1, and only when the backend actually reports it (diffusion steps, encoded
frames). Omit for indeterminate — the component never fabricates a percentage or
creeps toward 90%, because a made-up number is worse than an honest "still working".

aspectRatio.description:
Reserves the artifact's final bounds so nothing shifts when it arrives. Required,
not optional: a media placeholder that resizes on completion causes a layout jump
at exactly the moment the user is looking at it.

label.description: Visible and announced status text, e.g. "Generating image".

children.description: The finished artifact. Revealed when `status` is `done`.

events.name: onRetry
events.description: Recovery path for `failed`. Without it the failure state explains but can't be acted on.

guidance.engineering: The load-bearing decision is that progress is encoded spatially, not temporally. Each cell derives a stable pseudo-random threshold from its index (a deterministic sine hash, so the pattern never reshuffles between renders — a reshuffling field reads as noise rather than a resolve), and a cell resolves once `progress` passes its threshold. That is ordered-dither logic borrowed from halftone rendering: it produces an organic dissolve that is nonetheless an exact function of real progress, rather than a decorative animation that merely implies work. The payoff is the reduced-motion story, which is unusually strong for an animated component: because the information lives in the pattern rather than the movement, `prefers-reduced-motion` removes every transition and the progress stays completely legible — no fallback had to be invented. `progress` is optional with no synthetic fallback, deliberately: media generation genuinely reports steps (diffusion iterations, encoded frames) where text streaming does not, so a percentage here is measured rather than invented — the system's rule is not 'never show a number' but 'never invent precision you don't have', which is the same rule that makes Confidence Meter refuse one. `aspectRatio` is required because a media placeholder that resizes on completion causes a layout shift at exactly the moment the user's attention is on it. `processing` exists as a state separate from `generating` so a user is never told 'done' while an upscale or encode is still running. The requestAnimationFrame loop that drives indeterminate mode is not started at all when the component is determinate or motion is reduced, since an animation frame loop nobody can see is pure battery cost.
guidance.motion: Cells transition `transform: scale` at `--pd-duration-base` with `--pd-ease-standard`; because each cell's threshold differs, the resolve reads as a wave without any explicit stagger orchestration — the stagger is a free consequence of the threshold distribution. Indeterminate mode travels a phase offset across the same thresholds on a 2s loop, the single continuous animation in the component, and it maps to real ongoing work rather than decorating a wait. Completion is a cross-fade, never a pop: the artifact fades in over `--pd-duration-base` with `--pd-ease-decelerate` while the field is unmounted, so the two states morph rather than cut. Only `transform` and `opacity` animate, so the whole field composites on the GPU regardless of density. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` every transition is dropped and the wave loop never starts; cells snap to their correct scale and hold a static pattern, which costs nothing because progress was already spatial — the reduced-motion state is the same information without the movement, which is the fallback contract rather than a removal.

components.name: ghost-input
components.title: Ghost Input
components.description: A single-line text input with inline AI ghost-text completion: after the user pauses typing, a dimmed continuation appears past the caret, accepted with Tab or the right-arrow key (only when the caret is already at the end of the text) and dismissed with Escape. Takes a fetchSuggestion(value, signal) prop that the consumer implements against their own model — the component owns debouncing, request cancellation on every keystroke, staleness checking (a suggestion that doesn't continue the current text is discarded), and the accessible announcement of the suggestion via a live region. It never inserts text automatically; acceptance is always an explicit keypress. Use for reply drafting, search boxes, or any single-line field where predictive continuation should stay out of the way until the user asks for it. Not for multi-field or full-document autocomplete — this is a single <input>, not an editor.

value.description: Current field value. GhostInput is controlled — there is no uncontrolled mode.

minChars.description: Don't request a suggestion below this many characters.

events.name: fetchSuggestion
events.description:
Called after the user pauses typing, with an `AbortSignal` that fires the moment
another keystroke arrives. Must resolve to a full continuation of `value` — a
result that doesn't start with the current value is treated as stale and dropped.
Return `null`/`undefined`/`""` for "no suggestion".

events.name: onAcceptSuggestion
events.description: Fired with the full accepted value when the user accepts the suggestion.

guidance.engineering: The ghost text is rendered as a separate mirror div positioned exactly behind the real <input>, with the typed-text portion set to transparent — not as a styled fake caret or a contentEditable trick. This is the only approach that keeps native input behaviour (IME composition, selection, undo, autofill, screen-reader field semantics) completely intact, at the cost of the mirror div needing identical padding/font/line-height to the input, which is why both come from the same className. The whole request lifecycle — debounce timer, AbortController — lives in refs rather than state so that a rapid keystroke can synchronously cancel the previous request without waiting for a re-render; a state-based cancellation would let a slow response race a fast one and briefly show a stale suggestion. The right-arrow accept only fires when the caret is already at the end of the value (checked via selectionStart/selectionEnd), because otherwise it would silently hijack normal in-text cursor movement, which is a worse failure mode than requiring Tab.
guidance.motion: The suggestion's appearance is a plain opacity transition using duration.fast and easing.standard from the token scale — deliberately not a slide or typewriter reveal, both of which would misrepresent what happened: the whole continuation exists immediately (it was already fetched), so animating it in character-by-character would be a fabricated sense of the model 'typing', not a real progressive state. Under prefers-reduced-motion this reduces to a duration.instant swap via the same token path every other component in the system uses; nothing here required a component-specific reduced-motion branch, which is itself a signal the animation is doing the minimum necessary rather than something decorative.

components.name: human-handoff
components.title: Human Handoff
components.description: When a person takes over from the agent, and what they're handed. Takes a `stage` (`agentHandling`, `waitingForPerson`, `personHandling`, `returnedToAgent`), the agent's `reason` for stepping back in its own words, a `context` list of the facts a person would otherwise have to ask for again, the `person` who has it now, a `waitingFor` duration, and `onTakeOver` / `onReturnToAgent`. The context is the component, not the button: handoffs usually lose everything, so the customer repeats themselves and whoever takes over re-reads a transcript to find three facts. Listing what the agent already tried is part of that, since offering a customer the same rejected remedy twice is the most common way a handoff goes wrong. It also works in both directions, because handing a finished job back to the agent is the half products forget. Purely presentational. Use it in support, operations and any agent that can reach the end of what it may decide. Not for a single approval (that is AI Approval Gate), and not for a question the agent could answer itself (that is Agent Ask).

guidance.engineering: Stage is a four-value enum rather than a boolean because the return leg is a real state with its own copy, and products that model handoff as 'escalated: true' have nowhere to put the moment a person finishes and the agent resumes. Waiting is styled in the waiting colour with full stillness, the same treatment approvals get, so a queue of handoffs reads at a glance without a separate legend. The context list is `dl` markup rather than free text so a caller can render five facts consistently and a screen reader hears label-and-value pairs, and it sits inside the component rather than being left to a slot because the whole failure mode is teams shipping a handoff button with no payload.
guidance.motion: Nothing animates, in any stage. A waiting handoff is a person's turn and the strongest signal available is complete stillness; a pulsing 'needs attention' badge here would compete with the queue around it and train people to ignore it.

components.name: image-studio
components.title: Image Studio
components.description: A complete workspace for making images with a model, assembled from Prompt Composer, Parameter Panel, Generation Job, Variation Grid and Credits Meter. Takes `groups` and `values` for the settings that persist across runs, an optional `run` (status, queue, stage, measured progress, cost, per-result status), `credits`, and a `history` of past runs that each hand back their prompt *and* their settings through `onRecall`. The workspace is the design: generation tools are described as tossing prompts into a black hole, with a scrolling feed instead of an overview and settings that evaporate when you switch model, so the user ends up keeping a spreadsheet of prompts beside the tool. Here the settings sit beside the work and survive the prompt, the history is a recallable grid rather than a feed, and the price of the next run is named before the click. Presentational: you own the runs, the settings and the history. Use it as the whole screen of an image or video product. Not for a single generation in a chat thread — that is Generation Job on its own.

guidance.engineering: The layout encodes the three documented failures of generation workspaces. Settings live in a rail beside the work rather than inside the prompt, because the reviewed complaint about multi-model tools is that switching model reopens every consistency problem and leaves the user restating palette and framing by hand; a rail that survives the prompt is what stops that. History is a thumbnail grid with a recall control, not a feed: comparisons of the same review task put a grid at roughly five times the density of a scrolling list, and density is the whole job when you are looking for the good one from last Tuesday. Recall returns the settings as well as the prompt, which is the part a feed of images structurally cannot do. Partial results render inside the job rather than after it, so a finished image never waits for its siblings. The composer goes busy while a run is active instead of offering a second start on top of the first, and Stop stays on the job, where the run actually is, so there is exactly one place to end it.

The result is that the eye is drawn to the one region that is actually changing, in a screen that would otherwise have movement in every quarter. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` every part of that stops and the same states are carried by colour, position and words.

components.name: inline-citations
components.title: Inline Citations
components.description: Claim-level sources that take one step to check. `CitedText` takes the answer's `sources` (id, title, url, publisher, date), numbers them in order and renders a numbered reference list underneath. `Cite` wraps one claim, takes `source` (an id or ids), the `quote` that supports it (or one quote per source) and `support`: 'quoted' or 'paraphrased'. Each claim gets a small numbered marker. On hover, keyboard focus or tap, a popover shows the supporting passage itself next to the claim, says whether the source quotes it or the agent summarised it, and links to 'Open at this passage', which deep-links with a URL text fragment so the source opens scrolled to the highlighted words. The claim is highlighted while its source is open. A `Cite` with no source gets a dashed '?' marker and says it has nothing behind it, so unsourced statements can't pass for cited ones. Use it in AI answers, research summaries and reports. For 'why this?' about a whole answer, use AI Context Surface instead.
