guidance.engineering: Designed from one research finding: people rarely verify citations, so a numbered marker is mostly a comfort signal that makes answers look more trustworthy than they are. The design makes the check cheap enough to actually happen. The supporting passage itself appears in the popover beside the claim, so comparing the two needs no navigation. The link opens the source at that passage using a URL text fragment, with start and end words for long quotes because fragments must match exactly. Support is a tier, not a score: 'quoted' vs 'paraphrased'. A claim without a source is marked with a dashed '?' rather than left bare, because an uncited sentence sitting among cited ones borrows their credibility. Numbering comes from the order of the `sources` array rather than render-order registration, so it is identical on server and client. The popover stays in the DOM next to its marker, so Tab moves from marker into the link. It is displayed with the Popover API's top layer and fixed coordinates, which keeps it clear of overflow-hidden containers and transformed ancestors. Without Popover API support it falls back to fixed positioning. It opens on mouse hover after a short delay, with a grace period so the pointer can move into it, and on keyboard focus-visible or tap. Clicking outside dismisses it, and Escape closes it and returns focus. The always-visible reference list is the fallback where hover doesn't exist and the audit view where it does.
guidance.motion: Minimal, because reading is the user's turn. The popover fades in at `--pd-duration-fast` on the decelerate curve, with no scale or slide, so the quote is readable from its first frame. Hover opens after 180ms, so markers don't flash as the pointer crosses text, and closing waits 140ms so the pointer can travel into the popover. The claim highlight and the marker's active fill change colour at `--pd-duration-instant`. Nothing shimmers: citations describe finished content. All motion becomes instant under prefers-reduced-motion.

components.name: intent-preview
components.title: Intent Preview
components.description: An agent restates what it understood — and the guesses it made — before any work starts. Takes an `interpretation` (the request restated as one plain sentence), optional `assumptions` (each a labelled best guess, optionally with alternative readings the user can switch to in place), optional `boundaries` listing what the agent will deliberately not do, and `onStart`, which receives the confirmed values, plus optional `onRephrase` and `onCancel`. The guesses arrive pre-filled, so when they are right confirming costs one click; when one is wrong it is corrected with a native select rather than by rewriting the prompt, and the start button changes to 'Start with changes' so the difference is visible. The reason it exists: a model that misreads a request early builds every later step on that mistake, so the cheapest correction in an agentic run is the first one. Distinct from Agent Ask, which blocks until the user supplies something the agent cannot guess — this is for when the agent could proceed on its best guess, but being wrong would be expensive. Holds perfectly still, since it is the user's turn. Composes AI Action Toolbar. Use it before long runs, runs with side effects, or requests with ambiguous scope. Not for every request — adding a confirmation to a cheap, reversible action is friction that trains people to click through without reading.

headingLevel.description: Level of the title heading, so it fits the outline of the page it's placed in. Defaults to 3.

interpretation.description: The request restated as the agent understood it — one plain sentence.

assumptions.description: The guesses the agent made to fill gaps in the request.

boundaries.description: What the agent will deliberately not do. Boundaries are part of intent.

label.description: What the agent had to decide, e.g. "Dataset".

options.description: Other reasonable readings. When present, the guess can be corrected in place.

events.name: onRephrase
events.description: Send the user back to rephrase the request.

guidance.engineering: Built from the model-side view of how agentic runs fail: interpretation happens before planning, and an early misreading compounds through every step that follows. Surfacing the interpretation in one sentence, together with the specific guesses that filled gaps in the request, moves correction to the single point where it is nearly free. Two decisions keep that from becoming friction. First, assumptions arrive pre-filled with the agent's best guess, so the common case — the guess is right — costs one click, and the start label changes to 'Start with changes' only when something was corrected, so the confirmation carries information rather than ceremony. Second, correction happens in place through a native select of alternative readings rather than by rephrasing the whole request, which is both faster and more precise. Boundaries ('I won't…') are included because what an agent will not do is part of its intent and is the thing users most want to know before a run with side effects. It is deliberately distinct from Agent Ask: Ask blocks on missing information the agent cannot guess, whereas Intent Preview is for requests the agent could act on immediately, where acting on a wrong guess would be expensive.
guidance.motion: Still, by design. This is a user-turn surface under the system's turn-taking grammar, so nothing moves or shimmers while it waits — the absence of motion is the signal that nothing proceeds until the user confirms. The only motion is the shared colour transition on hover and focus at `--pd-duration-instant`, inherited from the composed AI Action Toolbar and the select's own focus ring, and it drops to instant under prefers-reduced-motion. Entrance motion belongs to whatever surface reveals the preview, not to the component.

components.name: live-status-line
components.title: Live Status Line
components.description: A single line saying what an agent is doing right now — the status bar of an agent run. Takes a `state` from Agent Presence's vocabulary, a `status` describing the current micro-action, an optional `detail` naming what the action is acting on (a filename, a query, a table), an optional `startedAt` that drives a live elapsed counter, and an `onCancel` shown whenever the agent is active. It replaces rather than accumulates, which is the whole distinction from its neighbours: Reasoning Stream keeps a scrollable trace, Chain-of-Thought Timeline keeps the entire turn's history, and this keeps exactly one thing — which is what makes it cheap enough to leave in permanent product chrome like a toolbar, sidebar footer, or table row. Composes Agent Presence in its `line` form for the indicator rather than reimplementing one, so the turn-taking grammar (motion means the machine is busy, stillness means it's your turn) holds here automatically. The status text is keyed so React's reconciliation runs its swap animation exactly once per real change; a re-render with unchanged text never re-animates. Layout is deliberately stable: the row holds a minimum height so changing text length cannot reflow its container, and the detail truncates before the verb does so 'Reading' stays legible even when the filename cannot. Unlike most components in this system the elapsed counter ticks internally rather than being caller-owned, because forcing a re-render once a second for a display detail would be a poor API. Use it wherever an agent's current activity should be visible without dedicating a panel to it. Not for the reasoning text itself (use Reasoning Stream), not for a per-artifact generation progress surface (use Generation Placeholder), and not as a general toast or notification.

status.description: The current micro-action. Replaced wholesale as work moves on — never accumulated.

detail.description: What the action is acting on — a filename, a query, a table. Truncates before the verb does.

startedAt.description:
When the run started. The component ticks the elapsed counter itself rather than
making the caller re-render once a second for a display detail — a deliberate
exception to this system's usual "the caller owns async state" rule.

indicator.description:
The indicator before the status. `mark` (default) is the agent's drawn head, whose
face follows the state; `line` is three dots, for the densest rows.

guidance.engineering: The defining constraint is that this component replaces rather than accumulates. Accumulation is what makes agent activity surfaces expensive — a growing list needs scroll management, virtualisation at length, and a decision about when to collapse. Holding exactly one line keeps it cheap enough to live permanently in product chrome, and pushes the history question to Reasoning Stream and Chain-of-Thought Timeline where it belongs. It composes Agent Presence's `line` form rather than drawing its own dots, which is the system's compose-don't-reinvent rule applied where it genuinely fits: the turn-taking grammar then holds here for free, including the fact that a `suggesting` or `awaitingApproval` status stops moving. Two layout decisions prevent the jitter this pattern usually has: a minimum row height, so text of varying length cannot reflow the container around it, and truncation applied to the detail rather than the verb, so 'Reading' remains legible when a long filename cannot be. The elapsed counter is the one place this system deliberately breaks its own 'the caller owns async state' convention — every other component takes progress, busy and duration as props — because a live counter would otherwise force the consumer to re-render once a second purely for a display detail. The interval is only started while the agent is actually active, and never when no `startedAt` was supplied.
guidance.motion: One animation, and it maps to one state change: when the status text is replaced, the new text fades up three pixels over `--pd-duration-fast` with `--pd-ease-decelerate`. Short deliberately — micro-actions can change every second or two, and anything longer would read as churn rather than as replacement. It is keyed on the status string so React's reconciliation fires it exactly once per genuine change; an unchanged status that re-renders does not re-animate, which is the same mechanism Progressive Reveal and Reasoning Stream use. The indicator's own motion is inherited from Agent Presence and is not duplicated here. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the swap is dropped entirely: text simply changes, which loses nothing, because the information was always the words rather than the transition between them.

components.name: media-result
components.title: Media Result
components.description: A finished piece of generated media, with its provenance attached. Takes the media itself as children, a `title`, an `aspectRatio` so the layout never jumps, `madeBy` naming the model and time, a `credentials` object (`attached`, a `detail` such as "Content Credentials + invisible watermark", and an optional `href` to verify), a `note` for usage rights, and `actions` with `onAction`. Provenance is stated in words beside the result rather than hidden in a details panel, and when credentials are **not** attached the frame says so plainly, because an unmarked file is the one a team needs to know about before it ships. That reflects the law as of August 2026: the EU AI Act's Article 50 and California's SB 942 both require machine-readable disclosure of AI-generated media, and the major generators now sign output with C2PA credentials and an invisible watermark. Purely presentational: you render the media and own the signing. Use it wherever a generated image, video or audio clip is presented as finished. Not for work still in progress (that is Generation Job), and not for a grid of candidates (that is Variation Grid).

children.description: The result itself: an `img`, a `video`, an audio player. Yours to render.

title.description: What it is, in the user's words: "Bottle on stone, warm light".

aspectRatio.description: Aspect ratio of the frame, so the layout never jumps while media loads.

madeBy.description:
What made it and when, formatted by you. Shown with the result, not hidden in a
details panel.

attached.description: True once your pipeline has signed the file.

detail.description: "Content Credentials + SynthID", "C2PA manifest signed by Acme".

credentials.description:
Content Credentials (C2PA) and any visible or invisible watermark. Since August 2026
the EU AI Act's Article 50 and California's SB 942 both require machine-readable
disclosure of AI-generated media, so this is a product requirement, not a nicety.

note.description: Your own note: usage rights, model terms, "for internal use".

UINode.description: A nested component: a name from this catalogue, and the props to give it.

props.description: That component's own props, matching its entry in this catalogue.

primary.description: The one action that takes the result forward. At most one.

guidance.engineering: `credentials` is a small object rather than a boolean because the three questions a team has are different: is it signed, what was applied, and where can it be checked. Treating the unsigned case as a visible state in the waiting colour — instead of simply omitting the line — is the deliberate inversion here: products that only show a badge when signing succeeds make an unsigned file indistinguishable from a file nobody thought about, which is precisely the one that must not ship under the 2026 disclosure rules. The frame is a `figure` with a `figcaption`, so provenance and title are associated with the media by the platform rather than by proximity, and the whole caption stays outside the media box so it is never baked into a screenshot of the image itself.
guidance.motion: Nothing animates: the work is finished, and this system reserves motion for a machine that is still busy. Only the standard instant colour changes on the action buttons, dropped under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

components.name: message
components.title: Message
components.description: One turn in a conversation, and the container the rest of an AI answer lives inside. `Message` takes a `role` ('user' or 'assistant'), a caller-owned `status` for assistant turns ('streaming', 'done', 'failed' or 'stopped'), and optional `author`, `avatar`, `meta` and `actions` (usually an AI Action Toolbar), plus `error`, `onRetry` and `onContinue`. Children are the turn's parts in the order the work happened: Reasoning Stream, Tool Call Group, then `MessageContent`. `MessageContent` styles plain HTML from any markdown renderer. User turns render as a right-aligned bubble. Assistant turns render full-width with no bubble, so long answers, code and tables have room. While streaming, text renders as it really arrives with a quantized cell cursor, never simulated typing, and actions stay hidden so nobody acts on half an answer. A failed turn keeps what arrived, says why and offers Retry. A stopped turn keeps the partial answer, labelled incomplete, with Continue. Use it for any assistant or agent conversation. Pair it with Message Scroller for the list.

status.description: Assistant messages only. Owned by the caller, from the real stream.

author.description: Shown above the message: "Assistant", a model name, a teammate.

avatar.description: A small avatar or an `AgentPresence` in its dot form.

meta.description: Timestamp or other quiet metadata, shown next to the author.

actions.description: Actions for a finished message, usually an `AIActionToolbar`. Hidden until it finishes.

error.description: Why it failed, in words a user can act on.

showCursor.description:
The end-of-stream cursor while streaming. Turn it off while something else already
shows progress (a reasoning trace, a running tool), so there's one busy signal at a time.

UINode.description: A nested component: a name from this catalogue, and the props to give it.

props.description: That component's own props, matching its entry in this catalogue.

events.name: onContinue
events.description: Offered on a stopped message, to pick up where it left off.

guidance.engineering: Designed as the turn, not the text bubble. An assistant reply contains reasoning, tool calls, citations and prose, and treating those as siblings of the message breaks both reading order and accessibility. Here they are children of one `<article>`, named 'You said' or '<author> said' and marked `aria-busy` while streaming, so assistive tech treats the turn as one unit that is still arriving. Status is caller-owned because only the stream knows it. Each status has distinct UI, and none discards content: failed keeps the partial answer (dimmed) with an actionable error in an alert region and Retry; stopped labels the answer incomplete with Continue and Start over. Actions on assistant turns render only once the status is 'done', because copying or applying half an answer is an error the interface shouldn't invite. The user bubble keeps its actions hidden until hover or focus-within, and always shows them on touch devices via `(hover: none)`. Assistant turns have no bubble so code, tables and long prose get the full width. `MessageContent` carries typography for the HTML any markdown renderer emits, so the component stays renderer-agnostic and dependency-free.
guidance.motion: The only moving part is the streaming cursor: one quantized cell pulsing on the shared `pd-cell-pulse` keyframe, the system's machine-busy grammar, rather than a blinking text caret, which would imply typing. It disappears the moment status leaves 'streaming', and the answer holds still once done. Actions on the user's own message fade in at `--pd-duration-fast` on hover or focus. There's no entrance animation on the message itself, because the list decides how new turns arrive. Under prefers-reduced-motion the cursor is a static cell and the fade is instant.

components.name: message-scroller
components.title: Message Scroller
components.description: The scrolling list of a conversation, which follows new content only while the reader is following along. Wrap `Message` elements with stable keys in `MessageScroller` and give it a height. It starts at the latest message. While the reader is at the bottom, new messages and streaming growth stay in view. The moment they scroll up, it stops following, nothing moves under them, and a 'Jump to latest' pill appears, counting messages that arrived meanwhile ('2 new messages'). Clicking it scrolls smoothly back down and pins again. When older messages load above (`onReachTop` fires near the top), the view compensates for the added height, so the page doesn't jump. Screen readers hear `announcement`, which you set when a message finishes, never per token. The region is keyboard-scrollable and named 'Conversation'. Use it for any chat or agent transcript. Not for feeds that should always show the newest item first.

announcement.description:
Text for screen readers when something worth hearing happens, e.g. "Assistant replied:
Churn rose in August…". Set it once a message *finishes*, never per token.

label.description: Accessible name for the scroll region.

UINode.description: A nested component: a name from this catalogue, and the props to give it.

props.description: That component's own props, matching its entry in this catalogue.

events.name: onReachTop
events.description: Called when the reader scrolls near the top. Load older messages here.

guidance.engineering: Auto-scroll is where chat interfaces most often break trust: a stream drags the view down while someone is reading an earlier answer. Here 'pinned' is a fact about the reader, recomputed from their own scroll position with a 48px tolerance. Following happens only while pinned, both when children are added (layout effect) and when the last message grows during streaming (a ResizeObserver on the content, since token growth adds no children). While unpinned, added children are counted into the jump pill. A smooth jump sets a guard, so the intermediate 'not at bottom' frames of the animation don't unpin and flash the pill back. A 700ms fallback lands on the bottom even if streaming moved the target mid-animation. Prepended history is detected by the first child's key changing alongside a higher count, and compensated by adding the height delta to scrollTop in a layout effect before paint. Native `overflow-anchor` is disabled, so browsers with and without support behave identically. Accessibility uses a named, focusable region for keyboard scrolling and a separate polite status for caller-supplied announcements, because a live log would read every streamed token.
guidance.motion: Following while pinned is instant, not smooth: animating toward a target that moves with every token lags behind and reads as sluggish. Smooth scrolling is reserved for the user's explicit 'Jump to latest', and falls back to instant under prefers-reduced-motion. The jump pill fades in at `--pd-duration-fast` on the decelerate curve when the reader leaves the bottom, and hover colour runs at `--pd-duration-instant`. History prepends are compensated before paint, so there is no visible jump. Everything becomes instant under prefers-reduced-motion.

components.name: overlay
components.title: Overlay Motion Primitive
components.description: The shared enter/exit animation layer for every overlay surface in the system — Dialog, Sheet, Popover and Drawer. Exports OverlayScrim (the backdrop) and OverlayContent (the panel, with a placement prop of center, top, bottom, left or right that controls which axis it translates from) plus a re-exported AnimatePresence. Not a standalone component: it has no dismiss behaviour, focus trapping or portal logic of its own. Compose it underneath a Radix primitive (Dialog.Overlay/Content, Sheet, Popover) so that primitive owns interaction semantics while this owns motion.

placement.description: Which edge the content enters from. `center` is Dialog/Popover; the rest are Sheet/Drawer.

guidance.engineering: Extracted as its own primitive rather than duplicated inside Dialog, Sheet, Popover and Drawer because those four are the same motion problem (scrim fade + panel translate/scale) wearing four different Radix primitives underneath. Without this, four components would each hand-roll slightly different durations the first time someone patches one of them, and the system's visual coherence — the actual point of a token-driven motion scale — degrades one component at a time. Deliberately excludes dismiss-on-click-outside, focus trapping and portalling: those are interaction semantics Radix already solves correctly, and re-solving them here would create two competing sources of truth for overlay behaviour.
guidance.motion: Two states only: scrim opacity, and content opacity+scale+translate along one axis determined by `placement`. Enter uses duration.fast with easing.decelerate (content is arriving, should feel like it's settling in); exit uses duration.instant with easing.accelerate (dismissal should feel immediate, not lingering) — this asymmetry is deliberate, not an oversight. The motion solves orientation: a Sheet sliding in from the right tells the user where it came from and, on exit, where it's returning to, which a plain fade does not. Reduced motion swaps the whole transition object for the shared `reducedMotion` token (near-zero duration) rather than removing the animation, so Motion's exit callback still fires and AnimatePresence still unmounts the content correctly.

components.name: parameter-panel
components.title: Parameter Panel
components.description: The controls beside the prompt: pick, don't describe. Takes `groups` (each a label and a set of `options` with a plain `label`, an optional `preview` thumbnail, a `costNote` and a `detail` line), the chosen `values` per group, `onChange`, a `summary` of what the choices add up to, and `onReset`. It answers the articulation barrier research directly: people can picture what they want but cannot name it, and style vocabulary is exactly the knowledge they lack, so options are shown as small previews they can recognise instead of words they must recall. Two further findings are built in: every option keeps a text label, because novel icons are misread almost universally, and any option that changes the price says so where it is chosen rather than in a bill afterwards. Purely presentational: you own the options, the previews and the pricing. Use it beside a prompt box for image, video or audio generation. Not for a settings page, and not for free-text parameters, which belong in Prompt Composer's controls.

headingLevel.description: Level of the title heading, so it fits the outline of the page it's placed in. Defaults to 3.

values.description: Chosen option id per group id.

summary.description: What the current choices add up to: "4 images · 1024 × 1024 · 40 credits".

label.description: "Style", "Shape", "How many".
Plain words, never a branded name: "Wide, 16:9", not "Cinemascope Pro".

preview.description: A small preview: a thumbnail, a shape, a swatch. Recognition beats recall.

costNote.description: What choosing this does to the price or the wait: "+20 credits".

detail.description: One line of help, shown under the group when this option is chosen.

UINode.description: A nested component: a name from this catalogue, and the props to give it.

props.description: That component's own props, matching its entry in this catalogue.

guidance.engineering: Each group is a real `fieldset` of radio inputs with the input visually hidden behind its label, so arrow-key navigation, grouping and announcement come from the platform rather than from a custom roving-tabindex implementation that would have to be re-tested in every host app. The chosen value is caller-owned per group id, which lets a product persist presets, share them in a URL, or drive them from a model's suggestion without the component holding a second source of truth. `costNote` sits on the option rather than being derived, because only the caller knows how its pricing composes — quality multiplied by count multiplied by resolution is not something a component can infer from labels. `detail` renders once per group under the current choice instead of on every option, which keeps a panel of twelve options from becoming a wall of help text.
guidance.motion: Nothing animates beyond the standard instant colour change on a choice. Selection is carried by border weight and label weight rather than motion: this is the user's turn, and a panel that animates under a moving cursor invites mis-clicks. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` even those transitions are dropped.

components.name: progressive-reveal
components.title: Progressive Reveal
components.description: Reveals a growing collection of items (rows, cards) one at a time as they arrive from a streaming or incrementally-loading source, with a stable layout and no per-character typewriter effect. Takes items (the current known array, expected to grow over time via the consumer's own state), a renderItem(item, index) function for the actual per-item markup, an optional keyExtractor for stable identity, and an isStreaming flag that shows a trailing 'More loading…' indicator while more items are expected. Each item is given its entrance transition exactly once: React's own keyed reconciliation means an item already present on a prior render keeps its existing DOM node and never remounts, so its animation can never replay. A layout prop switches between a vertical stack (default) and a CSS grid for card collections. Use for streaming search results, tool-call output rows, or generated card grids — any collection whose full membership isn't known upfront. Not for streaming prose (use an existing chat/response component) or a single changing value (that's Smart Field or Diff Accept's job, not a collection).

isStreaming.description: Shows a trailing "more incoming" indicator while true.

layout.description: `"stack"` (default) lays items in a vertical flex column; `"grid"` uses a CSS grid.

guidance.engineering: Enforces 'animate a new item in exactly once' by relying on React's own keyed reconciliation instead of hand-rolled 'already seen' tracking: each item is wrapped in a small RevealItem component keyed by keyExtractor (or index), which mounts fresh — and therefore plays its entrance transition — only the first time its key appears in the list; on every subsequent render where that key was already present, React reuses the existing DOM node and the component is not remounted, so the animation structurally cannot replay. This is simpler and more reliable than maintaining a Set of seen keys by hand, which is easy to get subtly wrong around React's own re-render timing. Scoped deliberately to structured collections (rows, cards), not prose — an append-only list of discrete items is inherently more layout-stable than a single growing text block, since new rows appear below existing content without reflowing it, which is also why this differs from and does not compete with Vercel AI Elements' prose-streaming components (see the roadmap's North Star Reconciliation table).
guidance.motion: Per-item entrance is a plain opacity + small upward translate (translate-y-1 to 0) using the same two-phase-mount pattern (mount closed, flip to open on the next animation frame) Command Menu and Selection Actions already use, on --pd-duration-fast/--pd-ease-standard. No item's own content is ever revealed character-by-character — the full item value already exists at arrival time, so a typewriter effect would misrepresent it as being generated live, the same reasoning every other AI-tier component in this system has already established independently. The trailing streaming indicator uses Tailwind's built-in animate-pulse (core Tailwind, no plugin required) gated by motion-safe:, falling back to a static reduced-opacity dot under motion-reduce: — the 'more is coming' text itself is unaffected either way, so the signal survives motion removal.

components.name: prompt-composer
components.title: Prompt Composer
components.description: A request composer that isn't a blank chat box. Free text for what only words can say, structured `controls` for what shouldn't need prompt engineering (tone, length, audience, format), and attachments for context. Each control is a labelled pill ('Tone: Friendly') backed by a native select, and a pill changed from its default is outlined, so the specification can be read at a glance. `onSubmit` receives `{ text, values, attachments }`. The text area grows with its content up to a cap. Enter sends and Shift+Enter adds a line, except during IME composition. Attachments come in through the attach button, drag and drop, or paste. You upload them via `onAttachFiles` and pass `attachments` back with status uploading, ready or failed. Sending is blocked while an upload runs, and the composer says why. `suggestions` fill the text but never send, the character count appears only near `maxLength`, and while `busy`, Send becomes Stop. Use it for generation features: drafts, images, reports. Not a chat input: no thread, no history.

controls.description: Structured parts of the request. The interface carries the specification, not the prompt.

suggestions.description: Starting points that fill the text for editing. Never sent without the user.

busy.description: The result is being generated. Send becomes Stop.

label.description: Visible label for the text area. Visually hidden by default.

clearOnSubmit.description: Clear the text after sending. Controls keep their values either way.

value.description: Controlled text, for filling the composer from outside (e.g. a follow-up suggestion).

label.description: Short label shown on the pill: "Tone", "Length", "For".

events.name: onAttachFiles
events.description: Enables the attach button, drop and paste. You upload; pass the results back as `attachments`.

guidance.engineering: Exists because the system argues against making every AI feature a blank chat box and needed an alternative. The composer splits a request into what only words can say (the text) and what is really a specification (controls), because specifications typed as prose are inconsistent and invisible until the result comes back wrong. Controls are native selects inside labelled pills, so they are keyboard, screen reader and phone friendly with no custom listbox. A changed value gets a stronger outline, so the non-default parts of the request stand out. Details are handled where composers usually slip. Enter is ignored while `isComposing`, so IME users confirming a candidate don't send half a sentence. The text area autosizes from scrollHeight up to 240px, because `field-sizing: content` isn't universal yet. Send is `aria-disabled`, not `disabled`, so it stays focusable and the blocked reason ('Waiting for attachments to finish uploading') is shown and announced. The count appears only in the last 10% before `maxLength`. The file input is reset after each pick, so the same file can be picked again. Uploads are the caller's, and the composer only reflects their status. It stays headless about what happens next: the caller assembles the prompt from `values`.
guidance.motion: Quiet, because composing is the user's turn. The only moving element is the shared `pd-shimmer` on an uploading attachment's 'Uploading' label, which is real machine work. Borders and backgrounds change colour at `--pd-duration-instant` on focus, hover, drag-over and control changes. The text area grows instantly as lines are added, with no height transition, so the caret never lags the text. Send swaps to Stop without animation, so the control is usable the moment generation starts. Everything is instant or static under prefers-reduced-motion.

components.name: reasoning-stream
components.title: Reasoning Stream
components.description: An agent's reasoning shown as it arrives — a two-line ticker while it streams, folding to a single 'Thought for 12s' line once the answer exists, expandable on demand to the full trace. Takes `steps` (reasoning summary lines, oldest first, appended as they arrive), `isStreaming`, an optional measured `durationMs` shown on completion, and `defaultExpanded`. The default is collapsed, deliberately: reasoning is scaffolding that is useful while a thing is being built and noise once it stands, and a reasoning panel left expanded after the answer lands makes every answer look like it needs justifying. Handles scroll anchoring correctly — it follows new content only while the reader is at the bottom, and the moment they scroll up it holds their position and offers a 'Jump to latest' affordance instead of yanking them back. Steps fade in whole and exactly once, enforced by React's keyed reconciliation rather than a timer; text that has already arrived is never revealed character-by-character, since that would misrepresent content the model already finished producing. `steps` is an array rather than a raw string because providers emit reasoning summaries as discrete parts and deciding where one thought ends belongs to the caller. Maps to OpenAI Responses reasoning-summary deltas and the AI SDK's `reasoning` part type, with no AI dependency of its own. Use it wherever a model exposes reasoning and seeing the work builds warranted trust. Not for the agent's activity state (use Agent Presence), not for the full historical record across a whole turn (use Chain-of-Thought Timeline), and not for a collapsed 'why this?' over an already-finished value (use AI Context Surface).

steps.description:
Reasoning summary lines, oldest first, appended as they arrive. An array rather
than a raw string because providers emit reasoning *summaries* as discrete parts,
and deciding where one thought ends is the consumer's business, not this
component's.

durationMs.description: Measured elapsed time. Shown once streaming ends — never estimated.

label.description: Verb shown while streaming.

guidance.engineering: The component's thesis is the fold-away on completion, not the ticker. Reasoning text is long, low-value-per-token, and usually not what the user wants to read, which creates a bind: showing all of it buries the answer, showing none of it is the black box that destroys trust. Collapsing to a measured 'Thought for 12s' resolves both — the duration answers 'was this worth waiting for' better than any amount of reasoning text, and the disclosure keeps the trace available for anyone who actually wants it. Scroll anchoring is implemented as a correctness requirement rather than a nicety: the component tracks distance-from-end on scroll and only follows new content while the reader is within 24px of the bottom, because auto-scrolling someone who has deliberately scrolled up to read something is the most hostile thing a streaming surface can do. That behaviour came from a competitive scan of a peer library's Message Scroller and now applies as a standing requirement to every streaming surface in this system, not as a component of its own. Each step is its own keyed child component so React's reconciliation owns the entrance animation — a step already on screen keeps its DOM node and can never replay its fade however often the parent re-renders, which is the same mechanism Progressive Reveal uses and which a timer-based approach gets wrong on the first re-render. `steps` is an array rather than a raw accumulating string so the component never has to guess where one thought ends.
guidance.motion: Steps fade in whole over `--pd-duration-base` with `--pd-ease-decelerate`, exactly once each. They are never typed out character-by-character: the text has already been produced by the time it reaches this component, and animating it as though it were being composed live would misrepresent what actually happened — the same non-negotiable rule Ghost Input, Smart Field, Diff Accept and Progressive Reveal all hold. The expand/collapse uses the house `grid-template-rows` 0fr→1fr transition at `--pd-duration-fast`, so no height measurement or ResizeObserver is needed and the panel animates correctly at any content length. The ticker's top edge is a CSS mask rather than an animated fade, so older lines dissolve out without anything moving. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the step fades and the expand transition are both dropped; steps appear instantly and the disclosure snaps, and since the information was never carried by the motion, nothing is lost.

components.name: response-feedback
components.title: Response Feedback
components.description: Thumbs with a reason that goes somewhere. Takes `reasons` (yours, in the user's words; a sensible default set ships), `onSubmit` receiving `{ verdict, reasonIds, comment }`, an optional `destination` naming where the feedback goes, `askOnUp` to ask after praise too, and `submitted` when you've already recorded feedback for this answer. A thumbs up sends on its own — praise shouldn't cost a form — while a thumbs down opens a small panel of reasons as multi-select chips with an optional comment, then a single Send. The confirmation names the destination, because a product that collects feedback without saying what happens to it is asking a favour it never repays. Purely presentational: you route the submission. Use it under an answer, beside AI Action Toolbar. Not for a support ticket, not for a rating that decides what the model does next, and not as the only route for reporting something harmful — that needs a path a person reads.

reasons.description: Reasons offered after a thumbs down. Yours, not generic ones.

askOnUp.description: Also ask why after a thumbs up. Off by default: praise shouldn't cost a form.

destination.description: Where it goes and what happens to it — the thing most products never say.

submitted.description: Set when the caller has already recorded feedback for this answer.

label.description: What was wrong, in the user's words: "Made something up", "Wrong source".

guidance.engineering: The asymmetry between up and down is the design: a thumbs up submits immediately and a thumbs down opens the reason panel, because the useful signal is concentrated in what went wrong and a form after praise costs goodwill for data nobody reads. Reasons are multi-select rather than a single choice, since an answer is usually wrong in more than one way, and they arrive as ids so the caller can route and aggregate them without parsing labels. The comment stays optional and is trimmed to undefined when empty, so a submission never carries a whitespace string that looks like feedback in a dashboard. After sending, the component collapses to a single sentence naming the destination instead of leaving the controls in place, which prevents the double-submit that turns one opinion into three.
guidance.motion: Nothing moves except the confirmation, which fades in once over `--pd-duration-base`. The reason panel appears without a slide or a height animation: it is the user's turn, and an animating panel under a cursor that is already moving toward a chip costs a mis-click. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the fade is dropped.

components.name: response-versions
components.title: Response Versions
components.description: Every answer the agent gave, kept. Takes `versions` (oldest first, each with `content`, an optional `label` naming what produced it and a pre-formatted `time`), the `activeId` and `onActiveChange`, plus optional `onRegenerate`, `onKeep` and `busy`. Stepping back and forth is two buttons and a count ("Version 2 of 3"); "Compare with previous" puts the current version beside the one before it, with the current one outlined; "Keep this one" hands a version back to you as the answer. Regenerating appends rather than replaces, which is the whole point: in most products regenerating destroys the previous answer, so a better answer is a gamble and people keep copies elsewhere. Purely presentational — you own the list, the regeneration and what keeping means. Use it under any answer people regenerate: chat replies, drafts, generated copy. Not for a full document's revision history, and not for comparing two arbitrary versions far apart in a list.

versions.description: Oldest first. A regenerate appends; nothing is ever replaced.

busy.description: True while a new version is being produced.

label.description: What produced it, in the user's words: "Shorter", "With sources", "First answer".

time.description: Already formatted by you: "2 minutes ago". Rendered as given, never recomputed.

Comparison is deliberately limited to the current version and the one immediately before it: an arbitrary two-version picker doubles the controls for a case nobody had, and the common question is always "is this better than the last try?". The compare toggle resets itself when there is no previous version, so a shrinking list cannot leave the component in a state it cannot render. The announcement says which version is showing rather than the content, so switching versions with a screen reader gives position, not a re-read of the whole answer.

Regeneration is the only busy state, and it lives in the button's own label ("Writing another…") rather than a spinner over the text, because the old answer stays readable the entire time. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the fade is dropped and the switch is instant.

components.name: run-inbox
components.title: Run Inbox
components.description: Every agent run in one place, with the ones that need a person at the top. Takes `runs` (each with a `title` in the user's words, a `state` of `needsYou`, `running`, `scheduled`, `done` or `failed`, an `agent` name, a one-line `note`, a pre-formatted `time` and an `unread` flag), plus `onOpen` and an optional `onStop`. The grouping is the design: an inbox is the familiar shape for background agents, and its familiar failure is strict chronology, where a run that has waited three hours for an answer sits below one that finished a minute ago. Here anything waiting on a person comes first whatever its age, failures come next, and each group carries a count so the size of the pile is visible before scrolling. Purely presentational: you own the runs, the routing and what opening one does. Use it as the home screen for background or scheduled agents. Not for the steps inside one run (that is Agent Plan), and not as a notification feed.

headingLevel.description: Level of the title heading, so it fits the outline of the page it's placed in. Defaults to 3.

selectedId.description: The run currently open beside this list, so the row it came from is marked.

title.description: What it was asked to do, in the user's words.

agent.description: Which agent, if you run more than one.

note.description: Why it needs you, what it's doing, or what it produced. One line.

time.description: Formatted by you: "2 minutes ago", "Tomorrow at 9:00".

events.name: onStop
events.description: Shown on a run that is still going.

guidance.engineering: Grouping by state rather than sorting by time is the whole component, and it is why this is not a generic list: the research on agent management interfaces names the inbox's scaling problem exactly, and a pile ordered by recency buries the only rows that block progress. Counts sit on the group headers instead of a single unread badge, because 'four waiting on you' and 'four finished' are different feelings and one number cannot carry both. `unread` only changes weight and adds a screen-reader phrase rather than driving a separate 'new' section, since a run's state matters more than whether it has been opened. Stop appears only on running rows, so the control cannot be aimed at a run that has already ended.
guidance.motion: Motion means the machine is busy: only a running row's dot pulses. Rows waiting on a person hold completely still in the waiting colour, which is the turn-taking grammar applied to a list — the eye is drawn by stillness and position rather than by something blinking for attention. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the pulse stops and state is carried by colour, position and words.

components.name: selection-actions
components.title: Selection Actions
components.description: A floating, selection-triggered toolbar for AI actions on a piece of text: select text inside a given container and a toolbar of consumer-defined actions (e.g. Explain, Rewrite, Translate, Classify, Extract) appears anchored to the selection. Takes a containerRef (scopes selection detection to one region of the page), an actions array ({id, label, icon}), and an onAction(actionId, selectedText, signal) handler returning a SelectionActionResult shaped as one of: { kind: 'replacement', value } which renders through Diff Accept for accept/reject review, { kind: 'text', value } shown as prose, { kind: 'classification', label, confidence? } shown as a label with a tiered confidence indicator, or { kind: 'list', items } shown as a bullet list. An optional onReplace(mergedValue, originalSelectedText) callback fires only when an accepted replacement is applied, letting a plain-string content model splice the result back in. Use for read or editable content surfaces where per-selection AI actions add value without a context switch to chat. Not for a whole-field or whole-document action (use smart-field or diff-accept directly for that).

containerRef.description: The region to watch for selections. A toolbar outside this element is ignored.

settleMs.description: Debounce after the selection stops changing before the toolbar appears, in ms.

events.name: onReplace
events.description:
Called only when an accepted `replacement` result is applied via Diff Accept.
Receives the original selected text alongside the merged result so a plain-string
content model can splice it back in (e.g. `content.replace(originalText,
mergedValue)`); a rich-text/contentEditable consumer would instead use its own
document model's replace-range primitive, ignoring the second argument.

guidance.engineering: Composes Diff Accept for the 'replacement' result kind (Rewrite) rather than reimplementing accept/reject a second time — Rewrite is exactly the 'AI proposes replacement text, human reviews' problem Diff Accept already solves, and the two components sharing one review UI keeps the whole AI tier consistent instead of each component inventing its own version of the same interaction. Selection detection listens to document-level `selectionchange`, filtered to whether the selection's anchor node falls inside `containerRef`, debounced (default 200ms) so the toolbar appears once the selection has settled rather than jittering while the user is still dragging or extending with the keyboard — one mechanism covers both input methods, since `selectionchange` fires for either. The toolbar's root uses `onMouseDown` with `preventDefault` — the standard rich-text-editor-toolbar trick — because without it, focusing a toolbar button would collapse the browser's live selection before the click handler ever runs, since focusing an element outside the current selection normally clears it. `onReplace` deliberately takes the original selected text as a second argument rather than assuming a plain string content model on the component's own side: this component cannot know whether the consumer's content is a plain string, a contentEditable region, or a structured rich-text document, so it hands back enough context (the exact original substring) for a plain-string consumer to splice correctly via `content.replace(original, merged)`, while a richer content model would use its own document API and ignore the second argument.
guidance.motion: The toolbar mounts in a closed visual state and flips to open on the next animation frame (a `visible` state lagging one rAF behind the selection existing), the same two-phase-mount pattern `Command Menu` uses, so the fade+scale-in (`--pd-duration-fast`/`--pd-ease-standard`) actually has a 'from' value to animate away from rather than popping in already-visible. No motion plays while the selection itself is still changing — the toolbar simply doesn't exist yet during that phase (enforced by the debounce), which is the correct behaviour research on floating selection toolbars confirms (centre after the selection settles, not during), achieved structurally rather than via a suppressed-animation flag. Result content (prose, a classification label, a list, or the composed Diff Accept panel) swaps in via a plain state change, never a per-character reveal, consistent with every other AI-tier component's 'the value already exists in full' reasoning. Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, the fade/scale transition drops via `motion-reduce:transition-none` (scale pinned via `motion-reduce:scale-100`), leaving the toolbar's appearance instant but still fully legible.

components.name: smart-field
components.title: Smart Field
components.description: An AI-proposed value for a single text field, shown with a confidence tier and its source before it becomes real data. The field's value never changes until the user explicitly accepts the proposal — clicking the trigger icon requests one via a consumer-supplied fetchProposal(currentValue, signal) function, which resolves to a SmartFieldProposal { value, confidence?: 'low' | 'medium' | 'high', provenance?: string } or null/undefined for no proposal. Once shown, the proposal renders in a panel below the field with Accept/Reject controls; accepting commits proposal.value into the field and shows a brief Undo affordance. Typing manually at any point (while loading or once a proposal is shown) cancels the in-flight request or dismisses the unaccepted proposal, since manual input always overrides an AI suggestion. Use for CRM/record enrichment, settings or profile fields, or any single structured field where AI has enough surrounding context to propose a value. Not for inline predictive continuation while typing (use ghost-input instead), multi-field or long-text diffing, or a consequential/risky action needing full review.

triggerIcon.description: Icon shown in the trigger button. No bundled icon set — supply your own, size-4 recommended.

triggerLabel.description: Accessible label for the trigger button.

autoPropose.description:
Fetch a proposal automatically once mounted, if `value` is empty. Off by default —
fetching without an explicit ask contradicts the AI tier's "nothing happens
unannounced" posture, but some products (e.g. Notion's Custom Agent autofill) do
want this, so it's an opt-in rather than cut entirely.

Changing this value requests a proposal. It exists so a parent can fill several
fields from one action — `AI Form Fill` bumps a single token and every field it
governs proposes at once — without this component giving up ownership of its own
proposal state. Ignored on first render, so mounting is never a request; use
`autoPropose` for that.

Confidence rendering composes the shared `confidence-meter` primitive (extracted after Selection Actions needed the identical tiered indicator) rather than hand-rolling its own bars a second time — a three-tier enum (low/medium/high), not a raw number, because a fabricated percentage would claim precision the underlying model doesn't actually have, and because the system has no colour scale to spend on a red/yellow/green treatment anyway. autoPropose is opt-in and gated to empty fields only, adopted directly from CRM-enrichment research (Clay/HubSpot/Attio): confidence gates whether a proposal is allowed to overwrite existing data, so the safest default auto-behaviour is 'only ever fill a blank,' never 'silently reconsider what's already there.' Manual typing at any point cancels an in-flight fetch or dismisses a shown-but-unaccepted proposal, reusing ghost-input's staleness philosophy: a suggestion answering a question the field no longer asks is worse than no suggestion. The proposal panel animates open/closed via a CSS grid-template-rows trick (0fr to 1fr) rather than measuring and animating an explicit pixel height, which is the standard token-free way to animate a height that depends on variable content without a ResizeObserver.

components.name: suggestions
components.title: Suggestions
components.description: Follow-up suggestions after an AI answer, where what a tap does is always clear. `Suggestions` takes `items` (strings, or `{ id, label, prompt? }` when the visible label differs from what gets asked), `onSelect(prompt, item)`, a `mode` of 'fill' (put the text in the composer to edit, the default) or 'send' (ask immediately), `streaming` (hides them while an answer is still arriving), and a `layout` of 'chips' (wrapping pills) or 'list' (full-width rows for longer questions). Fill and send look different, with a pencil or an arrow, and are named differently for screen readers ('Edit before asking: …' vs 'Ask: …'), so a tap never commits someone to words they didn't expect to send. The group is one tab stop, and arrow keys, Home and End move between items. Items arrive with a short staggered fade and then hold still. Use it under assistant messages and in empty states. Not for autocomplete while typing. Use Ghost Input for that.

mode.description:
`fill` puts the text in the composer to edit; `send` sends it immediately. Each looks
different, so a tap never does something the user didn't expect.

streaming.description: Hides the suggestions: follow-ups for an answer that hasn't finished are premature.

events.name: onSelect
events.description: Receives the suggestion's prompt (or label) and the item.

guidance.engineering: Most suggestion chips hide their most important property: whether tapping one sends a message. Sending words the user didn't write can't be taken back in a conversation, so the component makes mode explicit in three places: the trailing glyph (pencil for fill, arrow for send), the accessible name ('Edit before asking:' vs 'Ask:'), and the default, which is the safer `fill`. Items accept a separate `prompt`, so a short visible label can expand into a fuller question. Suggestions render nothing while `streaming`, because a follow-up to an unfinished answer is premature and often wrong once the answer completes. Keyboard behaviour follows the toolbar pattern already used in AI Action Toolbar: one tab stop with roving tabindex, arrows in both axes (so it works for wrapping chips and stacked lists), and Home and End. The active index resets if the list shrinks. Chips extend their hit area vertically with a transparent pseudo-element, and list rows are 44px tall.

Items fade in with the shared `pd-fade-in` at `--pd-duration-base` on the decelerate curve, staggered 40ms per item so the row reads left to right rather than popping in as a block. There's no slide or scale, so text is readable from the first frame. Hover colour runs at `--pd-duration-instant`. Nothing shimmers or pulses. Under prefers-reduced-motion the entrance is removed and items appear immediately.

components.name: thinking-experience
components.title: Thinking Experience
components.description: A complete agent run, orchestrated — the first Level 2 Block in this system, and the composed surface the AI-tier components exist to be assembled into. Takes one `state` from the agent vocabulary plus a `status` line, optional `reasoning` steps, an optional `ask` request, an optional `approval` request, and a terminal `result` with its action strip, then decides which of those surfaces belongs on screen at each moment. The value over rendering the same components yourself is entirely the orchestration: a consumer wiring Live Status Line, Reasoning Stream, Agent Ask and AI Approval Gate together has to re-derive when each appears, when reasoning should stop streaming, when the elapsed counter should freeze, and what happens to the machine's own surfaces while a human is being asked something — and that last question is the one most implementations get wrong. This block applies the turn-taking grammar at the level of the whole panel rather than a single indicator: when control passes back to the user, the machine's status and reasoning visibly step down in emphasis and whatever needs an answer takes a ring, while remaining fully interactive so a run can always be stopped even while it waits on you. Composes Live Status Line, Reasoning Stream, Agent Ask, AI Approval Gate and AI Action Toolbar, which transitively pulls in Agent Presence, Confidence Meter and AI Context Surface. Use it as the agent panel in a product — a sidebar, a drawer, an inline run surface. Not a chat thread and not a transcript: it shows one run in progress, not a history of turns.

result.description: The finished output. Rendered once the run reaches a terminal state.

headingLevel.description: Heading level for the question or approval shown during the run. Defaults to 3.

expression.description:
How much of the agent shows. `full` draws the whole figure beside the run, for
onboarding and consumer products; `subtle` (default) keeps only its head in the
status line; `off` uses plain dots, for dense professional tools.

guidance.engineering: The first Block in this system, and it is deliberately an orchestration rather than new UI: every visible element comes from an already-shipped component. What it contributes is the set of decisions a consumer would otherwise have to re-derive — which surface belongs on screen at which state, that reasoning stops streaming the moment control passes to a human rather than continuing to tick behind a question, that the elapsed counter freezes on terminal states instead of counting forever, and that a pending question or approval is what the eye should land on. The interesting decision is how the turn-taking grammar scales: at component level it is one indicator moving or holding still, but at panel level it becomes relative emphasis, so the machine's status and reasoning step down (indicator graphics fade to 40% and primary text drops to the muted colour, keeping text above 4.5:1 contrast rather than dimming it with opacity) while an interrupt takes a ring. They are dimmed but deliberately never disabled — a run must remain stoppable even while it is waiting on the person, and `pointer-events-none` on that region would have silently removed the Stop control at exactly the moment someone might want it. Emphasis is carried by a ring rather than by animation because this is the user's turn and stillness is the signal; animating the thing that wants attention would contradict the grammar the rest of the system holds. Ask and approval are passed as plain data objects rather than as slots so the block owns the decision of when each appears — a slot-based API would hand the orchestration question straight back to the consumer, which is the one thing this component exists to answer.

The machine region cross-fades its text colour and indicator opacity over `--pd-duration-base` with `--pd-ease-standard` as control passes between the agent and the user, which is the panel-level expression of the turn-taking grammar and the only motion that belongs to this block itself. The result fades in once over `--pd-duration-base` with `--pd-ease-decelerate` when the run reaches a terminal state. Everything else is inherited: Live Status Line's status swap, Agent Presence's rotation, Reasoning Stream's step fades and disclosure, AI Action Toolbar's colour transitions and busy spinner. Nothing is duplicated at this level, which is the point of composing rather than reimplementing — one rhythm, set once in the tokens, applied consistently by every part. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the block's own two transitions drop to instant and each child handles its own fallback, leaving the layout, the ring emphasis and the opacity difference fully legible without any movement.

components.name: tool-call-card
components.title: Tool Call Card
components.description: What an agent actually did — read a file, ran a search, fetched a page, wrote a change — shown as a record beside what it says. `ToolCallCard` takes a `kind` (read, search, fetch, write, run, call), the exact `target` it touched, a `status` (running, done, failed, blocked), and optional `name`, `input`, `output`, `error` and `durationMs`. It leads with a plain sentence, verb then target, and keeps the arguments and result one click away. `effect` defaults from the kind: read-only calls stay quiet, while calls that made changes or reached outside the app carry a label, because those are what a reviewer hunts for. `ToolCallGroup` folds a run's calls into one line ('Read 2 files, searched once, wrote 1 file') with counts of calls that made changes and calls that failed, and shows the running call in place of the tally. effect.description: Defaults from `kind`: read, search and fetch are read-only; write, run and call change things.

error.description: Why it failed or was blocked.

guidance.engineering: Built for a trust gap seen from the model side. An agent's answer blends what it retrieved with what it inferred, and the text alone reads the same either way. A visible record of the calls lets a reader tell 'the config sets a 30s timeout' backed by a read of config.ts from the same sentence with nothing behind it, and it makes failures just as visible: the demo's answer admits the docs fetch failed, and the failed card is right there. Three decisions keep this from becoming a log dump. The summary is a sentence, verb then exact target in monospace, so it scans like prose. Evidence (arguments and result) sits in a disclosure, capped in height with its own scroll so one large result cannot swamp the run. And effect is a first-class prop defaulted from the kind, so the handful of calls that changed something are labelled among the many that only looked. Blocked calls never ran, so they never carry an effect label. The group tallies only finished calls and reports failures separately, so the headline never counts a failed read as a read. Collapsible regions use the house 0fr→1fr grid with overflow-hidden, padding inside the min-h-0 child, and inert while closed.

While any call runs, the group headline swaps its tally for that call, so the one moving line is always the current action. Disclosures open with a grid-template-rows transition at `--pd-duration-fast` and a chevron rotation on the same curve. Hover colour runs at `--pd-duration-instant`. components.name: variation-grid
components.title: Variation Grid
components.description: The results of one prompt, with the good ones kept. Takes `items` (each with your own `preview` node, a `label`, a per-cell `status` of `running`, `done` or `failed`, and a `note` explaining a failure), the `keptIds` the user is holding with `onKeptChange`, `onRegenerateRest` which replaces only what isn't kept, a `regenerateCost` shown on the button before the click, plus `onUse`, `onMore` and a per-cell `onRetry`. Keeping is the point: research on how people use generation tools describes them keeping the two results they like and running the rest again, which almost no tool supports, so people download favourites and re-prompt by hand. Failures are per cell, so one timed-out result shows its own reason and Retry while the others stay usable. Purely presentational: you render the previews and own the generation. Use it for any prompt that returns several candidates — images, video takes, copy, layouts. Not for a single result (that is Generation Placeholder or Media Result), and not as a gallery of past work.

guidance.engineering: The kept set is caller-owned and passed in, because it has to survive the regeneration that replaces the other cells — holding it internally would lose the user's choices exactly when the component re-renders with new results. `onRegenerateRest` hands back the ids it is replacing rather than a bare signal, so the caller can keep positions stable and never has to diff two arrays to work out what the user meant. A cell that is still running is excluded from the replaceable set, which stops a second click from cancelling work already in flight. Per-cell status rather than a batch status comes from how these pipelines actually fail: partial success is the common case, and a grid that collapses to a single error state throws away results the user already paid for. The regeneration cost is a caller-formatted string on the button because unpriced iteration is the single most common complaint in this category.
guidance.motion: Only unfinished cells move: a running cell pulses its dot while the rest hold still, so a grid mid-regeneration reads as 'these two are working, the others are yours'. Kept cells change by border weight rather than by animation, since keeping is the user's turn and a celebratory motion there would be noise. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the pulse stops and the running state is carried by its label.
